implemented: NFR-DR-S-006 — full formatErrorEmbed implementation. src/internal/format-error-embed.ts replaces Sprint 3's truncate-only stub with the full sanitizer per the planner's pseudocode: (1) ANSI/CSI escape sequence redact via /\x1B\[[0-9;?]*[ -/]*[@-~]/g, replaced with the literal token `[redacted-control]`; (2) C0+DEL control char redact via /[\x00-\x1F\x7F]/g, replaced with `[redacted-control]`; (3) JSON.stringify the redacted string so embedded quotes become visible (e.g. `\"`) AND any stray non-printable byte that snuck past the regexes gets escaped; (4) truncate the JSON-stringified form to 120 chars + ellipsis suffix when over the limit. ANSI redaction runs FIRST so a CSI sequence is consumed as a single unit (otherwise the C0 pass would replace its leading 0x1B independently and leave the rest of the sequence in the output). The resulting public function `truncateForErrorEmbed(value: unknown)` retains its signature and is total — non-strings are coerced via `String(value)`. `summarizeError(err)` returns `{ name, message }` where `message = truncateForErrorEmbed(err.message)`.

assumptions.choice: Cover CSI (Control Sequence Introducer) sequences only — `\x1B[` + zero-or-more parameter bytes ([0-9;?]) + zero-or-more intermediate bytes ([\x20-\x2F]) + one final byte ([\x40-\x7E]). This covers SGR (color), CUP (cursor positioning), EL/ED (erase line/display), DSR (device status report), and the bulk of practical attacker-injectable escape sequences. DCS (\x1B P), OSC (\x1B ]), single-shifts (\x1B N / \x1B O), and other escape forms are documented as out of scope for v1. The bare 0x1B byte (ESC) outside any structured sequence is caught by the C0 control-char regex pass that runs after the ANSI pass.
alternatives_considered: Cover ALL escape forms (CSI + DCS + OSC + APC + PM + SOS + single-shifts) (rejected — over-engineering for v1; CSI is the dominant log-injection vector; the bare-byte catch-all from the C0 regex covers the leftovers conservatively)

Strip the ESC byte directly without an ANSI-specific regex (rejected — would leave the parameter bytes behind as garbage; e.g. `\x1B[31m` would render as `[31m` in the output, which is misleading because operators reading the log might think the brackets were the original input)

assumptions.choice: Redact control/ANSI FIRST (so the literal `[redacted-control]` token replaces the bytes verbatim and reads as text), JSON.stringify SECOND (so the redaction token is preserved literally rather than being JSON-escaped), truncate LAST (so the visual length matches the visible rendered embed). The truncation operates on the JSON-stringified length, not the pre-stringify length — the `"..."` quote pair counts toward the 120-char limit. A 118-char input produces a 120-char output (passes through); a 119-char input produces a 121-char output (truncates to 120 + ellipsis).
alternatives_considered: JSON.stringify FIRST then redact (rejected — JSON.stringify converts `\x07` to the JSON escape `\u0007`, so the C0 regex would never match the original byte; the redaction token would never appear)
Truncate the pre-stringify form (rejected — the visible rendered length wouldn't match the gate; a 119-char input post-stringify is 121 chars but the user-visible string sees 119 chars + 2 quotes)
Use a different truncation length (rejected — 120 is the planner-mandated value)

assumptions.context: sanitizeFileName separator handling — strip vs replace
assumptions.choice: Strip per the literal FR-023 text. The spec edge-case row gives `'../etc/passwd' → '_._etc_passwd' (or similar)` as an example, and FR-023's text is `strip path separators (`/`, `\`)`. Strip is faithful to the FR text; the spec example's `_._etc_passwd` shape would require REPLACING separators with `_` and is documented as `or similar`. With strip, `'../etc/passwd'` becomes `'etcpasswd'` (separators stripped, leading dots stripped, all alphabetics whitelisted). This is also what produces the planner's brief example outputs `'\x00\x07name' → 'name'` (control bytes stripped, not replaced).
alternatives_considered: Replace separators with `_` to match the spec edge-case row's example output literally (rejected — diverges from the FR-023 text 'strip path separators'; the FR text is canonical, the edge-case row uses 'or similar')

Strip separators AND replace inner non-whitelist characters with `_` (chosen — this IS the implementation; the strip-vs-replace distinction is only about separators, not the non-whitelist replacement)

assumptions.context: sanitizeFileName Windows-reserved check — split on first `.` vs last `.`
assumptions.choice: Split on the FIRST `.`. Per Windows file-system semantics, `aux.tar.gz` opened by name resolves to the AUX device because Windows examines the stem (everything before the first `.`). Splitting on the last `.` would treat `aux.tar.gz` as a `gz` file (not reserved); splitting on the first `.` correctly identifies it as the AUX device with extension `tar.gz`. This is the conservative choice and matches the planner's guidance ('with or without extension' in the FR text).
alternatives_considered: Split on last `.` (rejected — fails to flag `aux.tar.gz` etc. as reserved)
Check stem only with no extension support (rejected — would miss `aux.txt`/`com1.dat` etc., which are real attacker shapes)

assumptions.context: sanitizeFileName cap-at-255 ordering — before vs after Windows-reserved check
assumptions.choice: Cap at 255 LAST, AFTER the Windows-reserved check. This guarantees the Windows-reserved check sees the full input post-pipeline. If the cap ran first, an attacker could push a long string of allowed chars in front of `CON.txt` to make the truncated form `auxiliarystuff...something_long_that_truncates_to_AUX` — but actually this is impossible because the truncation is left-anchored (slice(0, 255)) so the right-side AUX would be discarded. The ordering choice doesn't affect the security contract here, but cap-LAST is structurally cleaner.
